title: His father Isaac William Howard and the candy shop
summary: Howard describes his father as a decent classical cornetist who ran a candy shop that did not pay enough.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Okay. Anything you remember about your father, that would be good. This is what we want to know. Can you get it up there and just --
Hold the mike up high and tell us about your father.

Well, I can't tell you much about my father. He was a very decent man. But he played the cornet, and when he got older, as he got older, oh, he used to play at Bajou's (PHONETIC) -- that's the wrong name. That isn't the right name. I can't say it. I can't say the name of the place
where he was playing.
Well, tell us about it and what kind of player he was. That'd be good.
Oh, he was a good player. Very good player, Buddy.
What kind of things did he play? Just go ahead and --

No, he played -- let me see if I can think of some of those things that he played. They were music that most people shun them, but I wouldn't shun them because I was raised with people like that, you know.
Uh-huh.
Italians, and he had an -- Italian.
he was an
Was he playing more classical, or like jazz or swing?
He played more -- not jazz, but classic, classics.
He was a classical player.
Classic player, yeah.
Like you?
He studied with Italian teachers,
Yeah, uh-huh. That's where he got that name from. Isaac William Howard.
Did he stay with music? Was that his way of making a living, or was that just like a hobby with him?
Well, no, that was just -- he couldn't do
no better. Because he had a candy shop, you know. A candy shop?
Yeah. He had a -- oh, I forgot to tell you about it. He had a candy shop, yeah, and he couldn't -- he didn't have nothing else but that candy shop to support him. Then --
(Inaudible) Hold the microphone closer,

Then, by playing music he got ahold of something else in music, I don't know what it was. I can't think of what it was, but it helped him play a lot, you know. And he got to play with Italians, and they are something else.
On the candy shop, now that was his own little store, business, place of business?
Yeah, a store, a little store.
And did that provide enough for the family, the money from the candy shop?

No, that didn't do enough. Father got out of it and got this -- what do you call it? The business -- it didn't pay enough money, you know, he had to get out of the business and get into something with more money.
I see.
That was the only thing about that.
Was that something you and your brother or sister had a chance to work in the candy store to help out?
Oh, yeah, we could work in the store, all right. Run errands and things like that. But we didn't stay around there too long. We didn't stay around there too long.
Were you and your brother and sister in music at that time?
No.
You were a little too young?
I was in music but my brother wasn't.
Uh-huh.
But I was in music a little bit. You have to take some of this stuff and throw out something that you don't think is kosher.
Don't worry about that.
That takes care of itself. The main thing is -- you know how in this case you get it and you use what you can, I mean whatever --
Did you hear what I said? Don't pay no attention to anything that's not kosher.
(Laughter)
